laneArtifacts.rawText:
## Overview:

This PR replaces per-ID `find` calls with one deduplicated `findMany` query. It reconstructs results in the original input order, preserves duplicate IDs, and converts missing rows to `null`.

The main risks for specialist review are whether `findMany` and its `in` filter match the database API, and whether returning `null` for missing users preserves the established contract. Empty inputs and duplicate IDs also warrant behavioral verification.

## Strengths:

- Reduces repeated database lookups and likely improves query efficiency.
- Preserves caller-visible ordering and duplicate entries.
- Uses a map for efficient result reconstruction.
- Handles missing database rows explicitly.

laneArtifacts.rawText:
- **[P2] Snapshot the requested ID sequence before awaiting**
  - severity: P2
  - why: `uniqueIds` is captured before `await`, but the result is built from the original mutable `ids` afterward. If the caller adds, removes, or reorders IDs while `findMany` is pending, the result can contain unqueried IDs as `null` or have the wrong length/order. The removed implementation consumed `ids` synchronously.
  - location: src/users.ts:26-26
  - side: RIGHT
  - in_diff: yes
  - pr_related: yes
  - confidence: 0.99

- **[P3] Short-circuit empty ID lists before starting database work**
  - severity: P3
  - why: For `ids = []`, the removed implementation performed no database operation, whereas the new implementation awaits `findMany`. With a slow or contended database, an inherently empty result now unnecessarily remains pending instead of resolving independently of database availability.
  - location: src/users.ts:24-24
  - side: RIGHT
  - in_diff: yes
  - pr_related: yes
  - confidence: 0.96

  severity: P2

  severity: P2
  why: `loadUsers([])` previously resolved to `[]` without accessing the database. It now invokes `findMany` with an empty `in` list, so an unavailable database or backend that rejects empty lists makes a formerly successful call reject.

resolvedReview.overview:
This PR rewrites `loadUsers` in `src/users.ts` from an N+1 pattern (`Promise.all(ids.map(id => db.users.find(id)))`) into a single batched lookup: it deduplicates the input ids, fetches all rows with one `findMany({ where: { id: { in: uniqueIds } } })`, builds a `Map` keyed by row id, and remaps the original `ids` array to the fetched rows (missing ids become `null`).

The rewrite is a clear improvement — one database round trip instead of N — and it correctly preserves the caller-visible shape: result length, ordering, and duplicate positions all match the input array. The residual issues are edge-case confirmations rather than blocking defects: empty input now hits the database, the not-found sentinel is normalized to `null`, and one query now carries one bind parameter per unique id.

findings.title: [P3] Short-circuit empty input before querying
findings.body: Previously `loadUsers([])` resolved to `[]` via `Promise.all([])` without touching the database. The new code unconditionally awaits `findMany({ where: { id: { in: [] } } })`, adding a wasted round trip for an inherently empty result, and on adapters that reject empty `IN` lists (or when the database is unavailable) a call that always succeeded can now reject. A trivial guard restores the old behavior: `if (ids.length === 0) return [];`

findings.title: [P3] Confirm `null` is the intended not-found sentinel
findings.body: The old implementation returned each `db.users.find(id)` result verbatim; `byId.get(id) ?? null` now normalizes missing rows to `null`. If this adapter's `find` resolves `undefined` for unknown ids, callers distinguishing `undefined` from `null` (e.g. strict `=== undefined` checks) see a changed return contract, despite the PR description stating existing contracts are preserved. `db` is not declared anywhere in this repo (pre-existing), so the previous sentinel cannot be confirmed from source — worth verifying against the actual adapter, or mapping to whatever `find` used to return.

findings.title: [P3] Confirm the adapter handles large `in` lists
findings.body: The change goes from N single-parameter queries to one statement with one bind parameter per unique id, and `ids` is unbounded. Many adapters cap parameters per statement (SQLite ~999 by default, SQL Server 2100); above the cap the single `findMany` fails outright where the per-id version did not. If large input lists are realistic, chunk `uniqueIds` into batches and merge the resulting maps.

# PR Review

**Verdict:** approve

## Overview

This PR rewrites `loadUsers` in `src/users.ts` from an N+1 pattern (`Promise.all(ids.map(id => db.users.find(id)))`) into a single batched lookup: it deduplicates the input ids, fetches all rows with one `findMany({ where: { id: { in: uniqueIds } } })`, builds a `Map` keyed by row id, and remaps the original `ids` array to the fetched rows (missing ids become `null`).

The rewrite is a clear improvement — one database round trip instead of N — and it correctly preserves the caller-visible shape: result length, ordering, and duplicate positions all match the input array. The residual issues are edge-case confirmations rather than blocking defects: empty input now hits the database, the not-found sentinel is normalized to `null`, and one query now carries one bind parameter per unique id.

## Verification

Verification was disabled: `pr_review_verify` (list) reported no user-level `verificationBaselines` are configured, so no baseline was selected or run. Disclosure: configured baselines execute PR code unsandboxed with POSIX-process-group supervision only — deliberate session escapes can survive it; use an external sandbox/container wrapper for untrusted PRs.

## Findings

### [P3] Short-circuit empty input before querying
**Severity:** P3
**Rationale:** Previously `loadUsers([])` resolved to `[]` via `Promise.all([])` without touching the database. The new code unconditionally awaits `findMany({ where: { id: { in: [] } } })`, adding a wasted round trip for an inherently empty result, and on adapters that reject empty `IN` lists (or when the database is unavailable) a call that always succeeded can now reject. A trivial guard restores the old behavior: `if (ids.length === 0) return [];`
**Location:** `src/users.ts:22-23 RIGHT`

### [P3] Confirm `null` is the intended not-found sentinel
**Severity:** P3
**Rationale:** The old implementation returned each `db.users.find(id)` result verbatim; `byId.get(id) ?? null` now normalizes missing rows to `null`. If this adapter's `find` resolves `undefined` for unknown ids, callers distinguishing `undefined` from `null` (e.g. strict `=== undefined` checks) see a changed return contract, despite the PR description stating existing contracts are preserved. `db` is not declared anywhere in this repo (pre-existing), so the previous sentinel cannot be confirmed from source — worth verifying against the actual adapter, or mapping to whatever `find` used to return.
**Location:** `src/users.ts:25 RIGHT`

### [P3] Confirm the adapter handles large `in` lists
**Severity:** P3
**Rationale:** The change goes from N single-parameter queries to one statement with one bind parameter per unique id, and `ids` is unbounded. Many adapters cap parameters per statement (SQLite ~999 by default, SQL Server 2100); above the cap the single `findMany` fails outright where the per-id version did not. If large input lists are realistic, chunk `uniqueIds` into batches and merge the resulting maps.
**Location:** `src/users.ts:23 RIGHT`

## Lane completeness

All requested lanes completed. The `correctness` lane initially returned `partial` in the batch; it was rerun to completion with the same tool policy and its evidence merged. The `security-performance` lane completed with NO FINDINGS.

## Strengths and notes

- Genuine performance win: collapses N sequential round trips into one batched query while keeping result reconstruction O(n) via the `Map`.
- Correctly preserves caller-visible ordering, length, and duplicate positions by remapping over the original `ids` array rather than the deduplicated set.
- Missing rows are handled explicitly instead of producing sparse/unstable results.

Notes: correctness — order and duplicate semantics are preserved; the flagged items are edge cases (empty input, sentinel normalization). Security — no concerns; the `where` clause stays parameterized with no new injection or trust-boundary surface. Performance — the batching is an improvement; the only residual costs are the edge cases above and the throwaway pair array fed to `new Map`, which is idiomatic and negligible. The repo has no test infrastructure at all, so the new dedup/remap semantics (duplicates, out-of-order ids, missing ids, empty input) are unverified — if coverage is ever added, those cases would pin this behavior down.
